transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Pinecrest Head of Product), Ravi Singh (Pinecrest CTO), Liam O'Connor (Eng Manager)

Summary: quick hosted API demo focusing on chat/text generation basics - streaming, key params, and retries. We also walked the Console for usage insights and touched on Redwood Optimize for batching/caching suggestions. Pinecrest asked about data retention, SOC2, VPC options and idempotent retries for spikes.

Topics covered: streaming responses; temperature/top_p/max_tokens; stop sequences; retry logic and idempotency keys; Console walkthrough (request logs, token-level costs); Optimize recommendations (batching, KV/prefix cache); security questions (SOC2, KMS, data residency).

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samir Patel on the Redwood side, with Lena Ortiz - we'll run through a short hosted API demo, chat + text generation basics. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Maya: Good, thanks. excited to see how this can fit in our checkout assistant flow.
[00:00:17] Ravi: Hi all, I'm Ravi - I'll be listening for scale and security stuff.
[00:00:22] Lena: quick agenda: 1) quick API basics and streaming, 2) generation params and examples, 3) retries and best practices, 4) Console + Optimize tips, Q&A. sound good?
[00:00:32] Liam: yep, perfect.
[00:00:38] Samir: cool, starting with streaming - so Redwood's hosted API supports chunked streaming responses via SSE style and SDK streaming. meaning you can start rendering tokens to users as they arrive which is important for perceived latency, right?
[00:00:50] Maya: mm-hmm, that matters for our UI since we show progressive answers. any gotchas for mobile clients?
[00:00:56] Lena: main gotcha is handling partial events and reconnects. we include chunk ids and sequence info in the stream; if a stream is interrupted client should retry with the same idempotency key or fetch the final completed response using request id. also note: streaming increases connection time but reduces time-to-first-token.
[00:01:15] Ravi: you mentioned idempotency keys - are they required for retries? what happens with partial writes?
[00:01:22] Samir: good question - idempotency keys are recommended for any non-trivial request pattern. for simple one-shot generation you can rely on client-side exponential backoff for 429/5xx, but for at-least-once semantics use an idempotency key so we can dedupe on our side. if the connection drops mid-stream, we surface a request id and a final status so you can re-request.
[00:01:42] Lena: also, server-side retries are limited - Redwood does automatic transient retries for a few internal errors, but we avoid retrying things that could double-charge tokens. that's why idempotency and request-timeout policies matter.
[00:01:58] Maya: okay, good. next, can you show the generation params - like temperature, top_p, max tokens? how do they affect cost/perf?
[00:02:07] Samir: sure. quick live example - (demo tone) here's a simple chat prompt and we vary temperature from 0.0 to 0.9. low temp gives deterministic answers; high temp = more diverse outputs. top_p acts as nucleus sampling. max_tokens caps output size which directly affects cost - tokens in response are billed. we also showed stop sequences for clean truncation.
[00:02:30] Lena: note on params: for retail recommendations you might prefer lower temp and narrow top_p for consistent suggestions. for creative copy we raise temp. also top_k available if you want fixed candidate sets.
[00:02:44] Liam: any advice for controlling hallucinations?
[00:02:47] Samir: combine lower temp with good prompt engineering and post-filtering. Redwood Optimize can run evals on a prompt set and flag regressions when you change model or quantization profile.
[00:02:58] Raman: [garbled] 
[00:03:02] Lena: (laughs) little background noise - moving on. retries - we recommend client retries with exponential backoff for 429s and a max attempt count. for idempotent requests you can re-send same key; for streaming consider resuming from last chunk id.
[00:03:20] Maya: how do you surface failure reasons? logs?
[00:03:23] Lena: in the Console you get per-request logs and a token-level cost breakdown. errors include standard HTTP codes plus an internal error field (rate_limit, capacity, model_unavailable). we also provide tracing hooks you can connect to internal observability.
[00:03:38] Samir: demoing the Console now - overview page, per-route dashboards, latency percentiles, and the request inspector where you can replay requests. here's a sample request log showing headers, model, params and the token counts.
[00:03:52] Liam: can we get CSV export of logs?
[00:03:55] Lena: yes - export or API access to logs for your account. we also surface per-token costs so product folks can see cost drivers.
[00:04:05] Ravi: security - we need SOC2, encryption at rest, KMS for keys, and VPC/private deployment options. what's available for hosted?
[00:04:14] Samir: hosted comes with SOC2 controls; we support customer KMS integration for sensitive keys and offer Private deployments for full VPC control. for hosted we also offer dedicated capacity (Redwood Dedicated) if you want reserved GPUs with isolation. I'll attach the security packet after the call.
[00:04:30] Maya: data retention - are prompts retained? can you opt out?
[00:04:34] Lena: by default we retain request logs for X days for debugging and billing, but enterprise customers can opt for minimal retention and audit policies. we'll include opt-out and retention settings in the security docs.
[00:04:47] Samir: quick note on cost optimizations - Redwood Optimize recommends batching small requests together, prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts, and quantization/model selection based on latency/quality tradeoffs. for example if you have short prompts we recommend frequent batching with smaller max tokens to amortize overhead.
[00:05:05] Liam: you mentioned KV cache - does that require special model modifications?
[00:05:09] Lena: models with autoregressive decoders benefit from KV caching at runtime - our runtime handles KV cache automatically on compatible model variants. you can also use prefix-caching to store common prompt prefixes which saves compute on repeated flows.
[00:05:22] Maya: any limits on streaming connections? mobile browsers?
[00:05:25] Samir: we support long-lived streams, but browsers can hit proxies/timeouts; using the SDK with reconnect/resume logic is best. for high-scale mobile we sometimes recommend a server-side aggregator to reduce open connections.
[00:05:37] Ravi: SLAs on latency?
[00:05:39] Lena: hosted doesn't have SLA by default, dedicated/reserved plans come with latency and uptime targets. hosted performance is predictable for typical latencies - we'll share benchmark numbers for your prompt shapes.
[00:05:51] Samir: now a short live sample where we stream a 200-token response, you'll see tokens arriving in chunks - (stream demo)
[00:06:05] [demo streaming sequence with partial tokens; small noise and a brief reconnect]
[00:06:38] Maya: okay looks good. question: on retries if we re-send same idempotency key and you dedupe, do we get the original response or a canonical one?
[00:06:47] Lena: if the original completed, we return the same final result. if it was interrupted mid-execution we either resume or retry a new run depending on status; the request inspector shows the canonical result.
[00:07:02] Liam: direction on exponential backoff params?
[00:07:05] Samir: start at ~200ms, double with jitter, cap at ~5-10s, and stop after 3-5 attempts depending on criticality. avoid aggressive retries that exacerbate hot spikes.
[00:07:18] Maya: can you share a short checklist for production integration?
[00:07:22] Lena: yes - 1) pick model variant and test quality on your prompt set, 2) instrument token-level logs, 3) implement idempotency + backoff, 4) enable prefix/KV caching where repetitive contexts exist, 5) run small PoC to observe costs and latency then scale.
[00:07:40] Samir: we'll attach a benchmark script and sample prompts.
[00:07:44] Raman: [inaudible]
[00:07:46] Maya: any final notes on billing granularity?
[00:07:49] Samir: billed by tokens for text generation + per-embedding unit where relevant; we show token breakdown per request in Console. dedicated customers can negotiate committed rates.
[00:07:58] Ravi: okay, sounds promising. timing - we want PoC next week to validate latency under our traffic pattern.
[00:08:05] Samir: great - Lena can run a technical deep dive / PoC kickoff. we'll need your traffic profile and sample prompt set.
[00:08:12] Liam: I'll collate and share the QPS distribution and request sizes.
[00:08:16] Maya: +1, we'll prioritize the checkout-assistant flow.
[00:08:20] Samir: excellent. quick recap of action items and owners - Samir to send pricing + security packet; Lena to share benchmark script and sample prompts; Ravi to provide traffic profile. we'll aim to reconvene for PoC kickoff early next week.
[00:08:37] Maya: thanks both, good demo.
[00:08:40] Samir: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.

End of transcript.
